## The death knell: a code that distinguishes sex, age, and mourning

In Almuñécar, when a bell tolls for the dead, the air fills with a message that almost all the older residents know how to decipher without needing to ask. The death knell is rung by rope, with two bells conversing with each other in a slow, solemn, unadorned sequence. There is no rush in this tolling: each strike is allowed to fade before the next one arrives, as if the bronze needed time for the mourning to settle in those who hear it from the street, from the kitchen, or from the fields.

The essential code is passed down by ear, from bell ringer to apprentice, without manuals or sheet music. In Almuñécar, two tolls announce that the deceased is a woman; three, that it is a man. This binary distinction, which may seem crude today, functioned for centuries as an instant parish bulletin: it was enough to count the strokes to know whether the impending mourning would be worn by a widow or a widower, whether the children left orphaned had just lost their mother or their father. The entire community found out before the town crier or word of mouth filled in the details.

The older bell ringers of Almuñécar, however, have added nuances that turn this basic scheme into a much richer language. The number of tolls not only indicates sex, but also approximates the age of the deceased: a young deceased receives a shorter, almost timid toll, while an elder is bid farewell with a longer series, as if the tower wished to count the years it takes with it. That variation is not written in any rulebook; it lives in the memory of those who still climb the bell tower and in the sensitivity with which they interpret each loss.

The tolling is interrupted during the religious service, a detail that reveals just how deeply this code is integrated into the liturgy and daily life. While the priest officiates the funeral mass with the body present, the bells fall silent: the mourning moves inside the temple, where silence carries a different weight. Afterwards, when the coffin is carried out to the cemetery, the tolling resumes with the same cadence, accompanying the funeral procession until the cortege disappears from the tower's view. That ritual pause is not an acoustic whim, but a show of respect that the bell ringers have always maintained, even when no one has asked them to do so.

The difficulty of preserving this code lies precisely in its intangible nature. It is not enough to know that two tolls correspond to a woman and three to a man; one must have listened to hundreds of funerals to distinguish the nuance that separates a child from an adult, a middle-aged man from an elder who dies in his bed surrounded by grandchildren. That auditory memory is built over years of exposure and with a sensitivity that no electric motor can replicate. The current bell ringers know this: when they are gone, the code will go with them, because there is no way to write down on paper the sorrow with which the rope is let fall at the funeral of a young person.

In the conversations still held in the bars of the old town, some residents recall how, as children, they learned to count the tolls without anyone formally explaining it to them. It was knowledge absorbed by osmosis, listening to grandmothers remark "they're tolling for a man" or "poor thing, she was just a little girl" as they leaned out onto the balcony. That communal learning, which turned every listener into an interpreter of the bronze, has been fading as automated tolls homogenize the messages and reduce them to a simple, unnuanced sonic alert.

The death knell is, of all the bells in the campanile repertoire, the one that demands the most from the bell ringer. This is not a festival, where the rhythm can be joyful and mistakes are hidden amidst the clamor; here, every strike is an act of solemn communication that admits no improvisation. The rope is handled with special restraint, with an economy of movement that reflects respect for the dead and their family. Veteran bell ringers speak of this tolling with a particular gravity, as if every deceased person they have bid farewell to from the tower had left a mark on their hands.

The community of Almuñécar has understood for generations that this tolling is not a simple notice of death, but a form of companionship. When the double knell sounds, the neighbors interrupt their tasks for an instant and listen, count, interpret. In that brief lapse, the bell performs a function that no mobile application has been able to replace: making the deceased's family feel that their loss does not go unnoticed, that the whole town pauses for a moment to acknowledge the void left by the one who departs. That emotional bond, woven from centuries of repetition, is what is at stake when the disappearance of manual tolling is discussed.
